result:
I think I'll write about the strange comfort of unfinished things.

There's a particular kind of peace in a half-read book left spine-up on a nightstand, in a sentence that trails off, in a sketch that captures a gesture but not the whole figure. We're taught to value completion—the finished project, the closed loop, the tidy resolution—but I find myself drawn to the open-endedness of things still in motion.

Maybe it's because unfinished things still contain possibility. A completed thing has settled into what it is. But the half-written letter could still say anything. The melody that breaks off mid-phrase could resolve a hundred different ways in the listener's imagination. There's a generosity in incompleteness, an invitation.

I notice this in conversations too. The best ones don't end with everything resolved. They leave threads dangling, questions hanging in the air, ideas that you keep turning over later while washing dishes or walking somewhere. The conversation continues even after it's technically over. It keeps living because it wasn't sealed shut.

Cathedrals built over centuries, the masons knowing they'd never see the spire. Gardens planted for shade that the planter would never sit beneath. There's something deeply human about working toward things you won't complete, about being a single chapter in a longer story.

I suppose I'm circling around the idea that maybe the goal isn't always to finish. Maybe it's to participate, to add your small motion to the larger current, and to be at peace with leaving the rest unfinished.

So I'll stop here, deliberately—
